title: Given a `List<Employee>`, collect the results of a stream into a list that cannot be modified afterwards, using either `Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()` or `Collectors.collectingAndThen(Collectors.toList(), Collections::unmodifiableList)`.
shortTitle: Collect employees into an unmodifiable list using toUnmodifiableList or collectingAndThen with Collections.unmodifiableList

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An unmodifiable list rejects structural changes such as add, remove, set, and clear by throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`. In Java 10+ `Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()` collects directly into a truly immutable list, and the portable alternative wraps a regular list with `Collectors.collectingAndThen(Collectors.toList(), Collections::unmodifiableList)`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya produces an official, finalised list of approved staff and wants to hand it out knowing nobody can quietly add or delete a name. She laminates the printout. The unmodifiable list is that laminated copy — read it all you like, but you cannot alter it.

**One line to remember:** `toUnmodifiableList()` returns a read-only list that throws if anyone tries to change it.

sections.s2_technical:
`Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()`, added in Java 10, collects the stream directly into an immutable list. Any attempt to call add, remove, set, or clear on the result throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. It also rejects null elements, which is a deliberate safety feature consistent with the `List.of` family. For example `names.stream().filter(...).collect(toUnmodifiableList())` yields a list that is safe to publish.

The portable alternative, which works on Java 8 and 9, is `Collectors.collectingAndThen(Collectors.toList(), Collections::unmodifiableList)`. Here `collectingAndThen` first collects into a normal mutable ArrayList and then applies the finisher `Collections::unmodifiableList`, which returns an unmodifiable view. A subtle difference: the wrapped view is read-only to its holder, but if someone still holds the underlying ArrayList they could change it, whereas `toUnmodifiableList()` returns a genuinely independent immutable list with no backing reference leaked.

A senior point about defensive design: returning unmodifiable collections from service methods is a strong practice because it prevents callers from accidentally mutating shared internal state, a common source of hard-to-trace bugs in banking systems where the same reference list may flow through audit, notification, and reporting components. I prefer `toUnmodifiableList()` on modern Java and the collectingAndThen form only when I must support Java 8.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's compliance service returns a finalised list of approved high-value account holders that several downstream components read. If any component adds or removes an entry, the shared list is corrupted and the bug is almost impossible to trace. This is exactly why an unmodifiable list matters — it makes the published list tamper-proof.

Problem 2 — Some services still run on Java 8 while others are on Java 17. This is exactly why I show both the modern `toUnmodifiableList()` and the portable collectingAndThen form.

The code defines `Employee`, a `ComplianceService` with `approvedNamesImmutable`, and a demo that proves a modification attempt throws.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh, Priya, Amit.

Step 1: `map(Employee::getName)` turns the employees into the names "Rajesh", "Priya", "Amit".

Step 2: `toUnmodifiableList()` collects them into an immutable list.

Step 3: Reading the list works normally and logs all three names.

Step 4: Calling `add("Intruder")` throws UnsupportedOperationException, which the demo catches and logs as a rejected tamper attempt. The list content is unchanged.

```
INFO: Approved (read-only): [Rajesh, Priya, Amit]
WARNING: Tamper attempt rejected: list is unmodifiable
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [Rajesh, Priya, Amit]
    │ map(getName)
    ▼
  Stream<String>: "Rajesh","Priya","Amit"
    │ collect(toUnmodifiableList())
    ▼
  immutable List<String>
    │
    ├─ read  → OK (logs the names)
    └─ add("Intruder") → UnsupportedOperationException (rejected)
    ▼
  Output: [Rajesh, Priya, Amit]  (tamper-proof)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — ComplianceService (immutable result) ═══

  ┌─ Two ways to an unmodifiable list ───────────────────────┐
  │ Java 10+: toUnmodifiableList() → truly immutable, no    │
  │   backing reference leaked, rejects null elements.       │
  │ Java 8/9: collectingAndThen(toList(), unmodifiableList)  │
  │   → read-only VIEW over a mutable ArrayList.             │
  │ WHY: defensive return → callers cannot mutate shared state│
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │       ComplianceService       │
  │  + approvedNamesImmutable(List)│ map(name).collect(toUnmodifiableList)
  │  + approvedNamesPortable(List) │ collectingAndThen(toList, unmodifiable)
  │      : List<String>           │
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │          Employee             │
  │  - name:String + getName()    │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. approvedNamesImmutable(staff)
  2.   → map(getName) → collect(toUnmodifiableList())
  3.   → immutable List<String>; add() → UnsupportedOperationException
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To return a list that callers cannot tamper with, on modern Java I collect straight into an immutable list with `Collectors.toUnmodifiableList`. Any attempt to add, remove, set, or clear throws UnsupportedOperationException, and it also rejects null elements, so the result is a genuinely independent immutable list with no backing reference leaked.

When I have to support Java 8 or 9, which do not have that collector, I use the portable form `collectingAndThen(Collectors.toList(), Collections::unmodifiableList)`. collectingAndThen first collects into a normal ArrayList and then applies a finisher that wraps it in an unmodifiable view. The subtle difference I always mention is that this is a read-only view, so if some code still holds the underlying ArrayList it could mutate it, whereas toUnmodifiableList leaks no such reference.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this returned a finalised compliance list of approved high-value account holders that audit, notification, and reporting components all read. Making it unmodifiable meant no downstream component could accidentally add or remove an entry and silently corrupt shared state, which is exactly the kind of hard-to-trace bug defensive immutability prevents. I prefer toUnmodifiableList on current Java and reserve the collectingAndThen form for the services still on Java 8.
